rv.q: What saves the production is its stupendous sense of scale and spectacle, combining to become something of a cross between Soul of Shaolin, Cirque du Soleil and The Lion King.
Although the three-hour yarn, with English surtitles translating muscular Mongolian verse, is overblown, repetitive and utterly alien, it is certainly something to behold.
It’s like King Lear told by Cirque du Soleil.
Too often they are redundant: a constant visual reminder of the misplaced excess of the production.
As spectacle it’s hard to beat. But this is one of those occasions when less might have been more.

But his trusted adviser Egereg, the real father of the queen’s son, is determined that his bloodline will inherit the crown. Egereg engineers a baby switch, with brutal consequences. The “go big or go home” approach of the show, which has been adapted for London by Timberlake Wertenbaker and is directed by Hero Baatar, extends in all directions.
The pace is punishingly glacial, but you don’t get the compensating artistic pleasures of, say, opera, ballet or a Shakespeare play for such a broad-brush, soapy plot.
Instead, it tells a short, thin tale of stupidity and cruelty at interminable length.
On its own terms, The Mongol Khan is a five-star show – and I’m already recommending it to friends.
A real sense that this was a spectacle you'd be foolish to miss.
The Mongol Khan invades the West End's biggest theatre with a show sure to set tongues wagging.
That said, this production is a spectacle, and a gloriously excessive one, and if you feel you’ve had your fill of stripped-back, minimalist shows, this is a show worth having on your radar.
What a pity there isn’t more real content.
The pre-recorded music is a horrible mix of bang, clatter and kitsch.
As baffling and bewildering as it is beautiful and breathtaking, it’s certainly unlike anything on a London stage currently.
It all feels big, brash – and empty.
The Mongol Khan is a spectacle in every sense of the word.
The Mongol Khan is an unparalleled visual feast that audiences who see it will feel very privileged to have witnessed.
However, if you can just park these considerations and go for the colour, energy and sheer spectacle you will have a great time.

Performed and crafted with precision and a “more is more” philosophy that is sure to be a crowd pleaser, this exciting and awe-impairing production will have many delving deeper into what the arts of other cultures have to offer, which is ultimately the biggest triumph the show could ask for.

cn.t: Critics praise the spectacular visuals and massive 70-strong cast, but find the story thin and dramatically weak. The show dazzles as a cultural spectacle, though many note it feels more like a tourism showcase than compelling theatre.
